title: With the Encouragement of the US Government: Petrodollars Lent Out, and a Warning from 1977

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The fee was the spread on recycling somebody else's surplus. Two oil shocks "created current account deficits in many Latin American countries" and "current account surpluses among oil-exporting countries", and, in the essay's own words, "With the encouragement of the US government, large US money-center banks were willing intermediaries between the two groups, providing the exporting countries with a safe, liquid place for their funds and then lending those funds to Latin America."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was concentration, and it is quantified. Total outstanding Latin American debt went from "$29 billion" at the end of 1970 to "$159 billion" by the end of 1978 and "$327 billion" by 1982. On the lenders' side, "by 1982, the nine largest US money-center banks held Latin American debt amounting to 176 percent of their capital; their total LDC debt was nearly 290 percent of capital." A loss on that book was not a loss of profit; it was a loss of the banks.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: There was no fog about the risk, which is what makes this node a foreknowledge node rather than a misfortune. "The potential risk of the growing involvement of US banks in Latin American and other less-developed country (LDC) debt didn't go unnoticed. In 1977, during a speech at the Columbia University Graduate School of Business, then-Fed Chairman Arthur Burns criticized commercial banks for assuming excessive risk in their Third World lending." The lending roughly doubled again after that.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall ran for a decade and the bill was presented to the borrowers. The essay calls the 1980s for Latin America "a period often referred to as the 'lost decade'" in which "many Latin American countries became unable to service their foreign debt", and records that the international response "ultimately helped alleviate the situation, albeit with some unintended consequences".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment was the workout itself, conducted through the IMF and the central banks over years rather than through any inquiry into how banks came to hold sovereign exposure at 176 percent of capital after their own regulator had warned about it in 1977. The essay records the response and its unintended consequences; it apportions no blame and no liability, and neither does this dossier.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Eurodollar market and a sovereign-lending convention that treated states as unable to go bankrupt, with deposits from oil exporters available to be lent on at a margin.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The decade-long sovereign workout apparatus — IMF programmes, rescheduling rounds and ultimately the Brady restructuring — which converted bank exposure into tradable sovereign paper.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Oil surpluses were deposited with the banks; the banks lent them to oil-importing states; the states' repayments depended on commodity prices and on rates the banks' own central bank set; and when rates rose, the exposure that had been the banks' profit became the reason they could not be allowed to take the loss.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Latin America borrowed recklessly in the 1970s and the lost decade was the natural price of its own profligacy — or, inverted, that the whole episode was a deliberate plot to capture the continent through debt.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The profligacy reading omits who arranged the lending and on whose encouragement. The essay records that the recycling of oil surpluses into Latin American debt was done by large US money-center banks acting "With the encouragement of the US government", and that by 1982 those banks held Latin American debt at 176 percent of their capital — a structure built by lenders, not only by borrowers. The plot reading fails on the 1977 warning: if the exposure had been designed as a trap, the Federal Reserve chairman criticising commercial banks publicly "for assuming excessive risk in their Third World lending" five years before the default would be an odd move. What the record shows is a known risk that was named by the regulator and run anyway because it was profitable.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Oil shocks producing matched deficits and surpluses; US money-center banks intermediating between them with the encouragement of the US government. Debt rising from $29 billion at the end of 1970 to $159 billion by the end of 1978 and $327 billion by 1982. A public warning by Fed Chairman Arthur Burns at Columbia in 1977 about commercial banks assuming excessive risk in Third World lending. Nine largest money-center banks holding Latin American debt at 176 percent of capital and total less-developed-country debt at nearly 290 percent of capital by 1982. And a decade in which many of the borrowing countries could not service the debt, with an international response that helped "albeit with some unintended consequences".

citations.title: Federal Reserve History, "Latin American Debt Crisis of the 1980s, 1982-1989", by Jocelyn Sims and Jessie Romero
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from federalreservehistory.org. On the recycling mechanism: "During the 1970s, two large oil price shocks created current account deficits in many Latin American countries. At the same time, these shocks created current account surpluses among oil-exporting countries. With the encouragement of the US government, large US money-center banks were willing intermediaries between the two groups, providing the exporting countries with a safe, liquid place for their funds and then lending those funds to Latin America." The phrase "With the encouragement of the US government" is the essay's. On the scale: "At the end of 1970, total outstanding debt from all sources totaled only $29 billion, but by the end of 1978, that number had skyrocketed to $159 billion. By 1982, the debt level reached $327 billion." THE WARNING ON THE RECORD, and its date: "The potential risk of the growing involvement of US banks in Latin American and other less-developed country (LDC) debt didn't go unnoticed. In 1977, during a speech at the Columbia University Graduate School of Business, then-Fed Chairman Arthur Burns criticized commercial banks for assuming excessive risk in their Third World lending." And what happened anyway: "Still, by 1982, the nine largest US money-center banks held Latin American debt amounting to 176 percent of their capital; their total LDC debt was nearly 290 percent of capital." The essay describes the decade as one "often referred to as the 'lost decade'" in which "many Latin American countries became unable to service their foreign debt", and says the international response "ultimately helped alleviate the situation, albeit with some unintended consequences." SOURCE CHARACTER: Federal Reserve History is an educational project of the Federal Reserve System. This is a signed secondary essay with its own bibliography, not a primary record, and it is tiered and attributed accordingly: the dossier says what the essay states, not what a contemporaneous document shows.
